name: Application Security
description: OWASP Top 10, secure SDLC, dependency and supply-chain risk, and the tooling that finds bugs before attackers do.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Application Security is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is application security (AppSec)?
cards.answer: Making the software itself secure: designing, writing, testing and maintaining applications so that attackers cannot misuse them to steal data or take control — as opposed to securing the network or machines around them.
cards.explanation: Most breaches of web applications exploit bugs in the application's own code or its dependencies, so security has to be part of how software is built, not bolted on afterwards.

cards.prompt: What is OWASP, and what is the OWASP Top 10?
cards.answer: OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) is a non-profit community producing free security guidance and tools. Its Top 10 is a regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks — a common starting checklist.
cards.explanation: The Top 10 is an awareness document, not a complete standard; OWASP's ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard) is the detailed checklist for verifying an application.

cards.prompt: Why is "never trust user input" the first rule of application security?
cards.answer: Anything that comes from outside — form fields, URLs, headers, cookies, uploaded files, API payloads — can be crafted by an attacker. If the application treats that data as code or as trusted, it can be made to do things it should not.
cards.explanation: Injection attacks (SQL injection, cross-site scripting, command injection) all come from mixing untrusted data into something that gets interpreted. The defence is validating input and keeping data separate from code — for example with parameterised queries.

cards.prompt: What is SQL injection, in one sentence, and how do you prevent it?
cards.answer: An attack where user input is pasted into a SQL query string and changes the query's meaning — `' OR 1=1 --` in a login form can bypass the password check. Prevent it with parameterised queries (prepared statements), never string concatenation.
cards.explanation: Parameterised queries send the SQL and the data separately, so the database never interprets data as SQL. Every mainstream database library supports them.

resources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet — SQL injection prevention

cards.prompt: Why must secrets never be committed to source code?
cards.answer: Passwords, API keys and private keys in a repository are visible to everyone with access and stay in its history forever — bots scan public repositories for leaked keys within minutes.
cards.explanation: Keep secrets in environment variables or a secrets manager, add secret scanning to CI, and if one does leak, rotate it immediately: deleting the commit is not enough.

cards.prompt: What does "shift left" mean in security?
cards.answer: Moving security work earlier in the development process — threat modelling during design, secure coding guidance, automated scanning in the editor and CI — instead of only testing once the software is finished.
cards.explanation: A design flaw found on a whiteboard costs minutes to fix; the same flaw found in production costs an incident. Automated tools (SAST, dependency scanning) in CI catch common mistakes on every change.

modules.name: OWASP Top 10 in Practice
modules.description: The categories that account for most real-world web vulnerabilities.

cards.prompt: Name the OWASP Top 10 (2025) categories.
cards.answer: A01 Broken access control, A02 Security misconfiguration, A03 Software supply chain failures, A04 Cryptographic failures, A05 Injection, A06 Insecure design, A07 Authentication failures, A08 Software or data integrity failures, A09 Security logging and alerting failures, A10 Mishandling of exceptional conditions.
cards.explanation: It is a ranked awareness document, not a coverage checklist. Compared with 2021, supply-chain failures became their own category, SSRF was folded into broken access control, and mishandling of exceptional conditions (failing open, leaking errors) is new — a sign that most serious breaches now come from design, configuration and dependencies rather than a single missing escape function.

cards.prompt: What is the vulnerability here?
cards.answer: Insecure direct object reference: the user is authenticated but never authorised for *this* invoice. Any logged-in user can read any invoice by changing the id. Scope the query to the owner.
cards.explanation: IDOR is the most common instance of A01. The robust fix is to make ownership part of the query (`{'_id': id, 'owner': current_user.id}`) rather than a separate check someone will forget. Unguessable ids are not access control.

resources.title: OWASP — Insecure direct object reference prevention

cards.prompt: Injection is not just SQL. Name the other common forms and the single underlying fix.
cards.answer: Command injection, LDAP, XPath, NoSQL, template injection, log injection, header injection and prompt injection. The underlying fix is always the same: never let untrusted data cross into a position where it is interpreted as code — use parameterisation or a safe API, not escaping.
cards.explanation: Whenever you build a string that another interpreter will parse, you have an injection risk. `subprocess.run([...], shell=False)` beats string concatenation; a template engine with autoescape beats manual escaping; a query builder beats format strings.

cards.prompt: Why is `pickle.loads(user_data)` (or Java native deserialization) a critical vulnerability?
cards.answer: Those formats can reconstruct arbitrary objects and invoke code during deserialization, so untrusted input becomes remote code execution. Use a data-only format — JSON with a schema — and never deserialize untrusted data into live objects.
cards.explanation: Gadget chains make this exploitable even without an obvious `__reduce__`: attackers assemble classes already on your classpath. Log4Shell was a variant of the same theme — untrusted data reaching an interpreter with more power than expected.

cards.prompt: What should security logging capture — and what must it never contain?
cards.answer: Capture authentication successes and failures, access-control denials, privilege changes, input validation failures, and administrative actions — each with who, what, when, from where, and a correlation id. Never log passwords, tokens, full card numbers, or unredacted personal data.
cards.explanation: A09 exists because the average breach goes undetected for months. Logs must also be tamper-resistant (ship them off the host) and monitored — an unread log is an expensive way to store disappointment.

modules.name: Secure SDLC & Supply Chain
modules.description: Shifting security left, dependency risk and the tooling that scales.

cards.prompt: SAST vs DAST vs SCA
cards.answer: SAST analyses source without running it, DAST attacks the running application, SCA inventories your dependencies and flags known CVEs.

left.title: SAST
points: Runs on every commit, finds issues early
Sees all code paths, including rare ones
Cannot see runtime or config issues

right.title: DAST / SCA
points: DAST: real requests, real responses — few false positives
DAST: only exercises what it can reach
SCA: cheapest high-value scan there is
SCA: needs a real fix path, not just a report

cards.explanation: Start with SCA — known-vulnerable dependencies are the highest-yield, lowest-effort category. Then SAST on diffs only (full-repo scans produce backlog fatigue), then DAST in staging. Tools find bug classes; threat modelling finds design flaws.

cards.prompt: What are the main software supply-chain risks, and what reduces them?
cards.answer: Typosquatted or hijacked packages, malicious post-install scripts, compromised build systems, and unpinned transitive dependencies. Reduce them with lockfiles, pinned digests, dependency review, disabled install scripts, an SBOM, artefact signing and reproducible builds.
cards.explanation: SolarWinds and the xz backdoor showed the build system itself is a target. SLSA gives a maturity ladder; the practical first steps are pinning by hash, minimising dependencies, and keeping CI credentials scoped and short-lived.

resources.title: SLSA — Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts

cards.prompt: What should you check before adding a dependency?
cards.answer: Maintenance activity and maintainer count, open critical issues, transitive dependency count, licence compatibility, install-script behaviour, download provenance — and whether ten lines of your own code would do the job.
cards.explanation: Every dependency is code you ship, an update treadmill and an attack surface. `left-pad` and `event-stream` were both small packages. The rule of thumb: the smaller the utility, the higher the bar for pulling it in.

cards.prompt: Where does input validation belong, and should it be an allowlist or a denylist?
cards.answer: On the server, at the trust boundary, always — client-side validation is a UX feature. Use an allowlist: define what is valid and reject everything else. Denylists are always incomplete.
cards.explanation: Validate structure and type at the edge (a schema library such as Zod or Pydantic), then encode contextually at every output sink. Validation and encoding are different jobs; doing only one of them is where injection bugs live.

modules.name: Vulnerability Classes in Code
modules.description: Path traversal, command injection, file uploads, XXE, template injection, mass assignment, open redirects and TOCTOU races.

cards.prompt: What can an attacker read with `?name=../../etc/passwd`?
cards.answer: Any file the process can access: `../` sequences escape the uploads directory (path traversal). Resolve the final path and verify it is still inside the base directory — `(BASE / name).resolve().is_relative_to(BASE)` — or better, never use user input as a filename: look files up by an ID.
cards.explanation: Naive filters that strip `../` fail against encodings (`%2e%2e%2f`), absolute paths and double-dot variants. Canonicalise first, then check containment. Running with minimal filesystem permissions limits the damage when a check is missed.

cards.prompt: Why is this exploitable, and what is the safe version?
cards.answer: With `shell=True` the string is interpreted by a shell, so `host=example.com; rm -rf /` runs a second command. Pass an argument list without a shell — `subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host])` — and validate `host` against an allowlist pattern; add `--` where the tool supports it so input cannot become an option.
cards.explanation: Without a shell there are no metacharacters to abuse, but argument injection remains possible: a value beginning with `-` can be parsed as a flag. Better still, use a library API instead of shelling out at all.

resources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet — OS Command Injection Defense

cards.prompt: What are the rules for accepting file uploads safely?
cards.answer: Allowlist extensions and verify content type by inspecting the file, not trusting the client's header; limit size; generate your own random filename; store outside the web root (ideally object storage on a separate domain); never execute or include uploaded files; scan for malware; and serve with `Content-Disposition: attachment` and `nosniff`.
cards.explanation: Uploaded HTML or SVG served from your own origin is stored XSS; an uploaded `.php` in the web root is remote code execution. Image-processing libraries parsing hostile files have their own vulnerabilities, so keep them patched and process uploads in isolation.

cards.prompt: What is XXE, and how do you prevent it?
cards.answer: XML External Entity injection: an XML document defines an entity pointing at a file or URL (`<!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">`), and a permissive parser expands it — leaking files, performing SSRF, or exhausting memory ("billion laughs"). Disable DTDs and external entity resolution in the parser.
cards.explanation: Many XML libraries historically enabled these features by default. Use hardened parsers (Python's `defusedxml`), or prefer JSON when you control the format. Remember XML hides inside DOCX, SVG and SAML.

resources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet — XML External Entity Prevention

cards.prompt: Why is rendering this greeting a remote-code-execution risk?
cards.answer: User input is concatenated into the template *source*, so `{{ ... }}` expressions the user supplies are evaluated by the template engine — server-side template injection. Keep templates fixed and pass user data as variables: `render_template_string("Hello {{ name }}", name=name)`.
cards.explanation: Template engines expose object graphs powerful enough to reach the OS from an expression, so SSTI is usually full RCE. The general rule for every injection class: data goes in parameters, never into the code or query text itself.

resources.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Server-side template injection

cards.prompt: What can a user do by sending `{"name": "x", "is_admin": true}`?
cards.answer: Mass assignment: every field in the request body is copied onto the model, so the user makes themselves an administrator — or changes their balance, owner ID or verification status. Bind only an explicit allowlist of fields, using a dedicated input DTO or schema for each endpoint.
cards.explanation: Separate input models from database models. Frameworks offer tools — Pydantic request models, `[Bind]` attributes, strong parameters — but they only help if the allowlist is the default rather than something someone has to remember.

cards.prompt: What is an open redirect, and why does it matter?
cards.answer: An endpoint like `/login?next=https://evil.example` that redirects wherever a parameter says. Attackers use your trusted domain in phishing links, and in OAuth flows an open redirect can leak authorisation codes or tokens.
cards.explanation: Only redirect to relative paths or an allowlist of destinations; reject protocol-relative `//evil.example` and backslash tricks, which browsers treat as absolute URLs. Validate after parsing the URL, not with string prefix checks.

resources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet — Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards

cards.prompt: A gift card worth £50 is redeemed twenty times by sending twenty simultaneous requests. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
cards.answer: A check-then-act race: each request read "balance £50, not redeemed" before any of them wrote the update. Make the check and update atomic — a conditional update (`UPDATE cards SET redeemed = true WHERE id = ? AND redeemed = false`, then check rows affected), row locks, or a unique constraint.
cards.explanation: Business-logic races (double spending, coupon reuse, bypassing limits) are found by firing parallel requests, which tools such as Burp's single-packet attack make easy. Anything involving money, quotas or one-time use needs atomicity at the data layer.

resources.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Race conditions

modules.name: Secure Development Practice
modules.description: Standards and code review, secure defaults and error handling, secrets, security tests and threat-driven design.

cards.prompt: What is OWASP ASVS, and how does it differ from the Top 10?
cards.answer: The Application Security Verification Standard is a detailed list of testable security requirements — authentication, session management, access control, validation, cryptography, logging and more — organised into three levels by assurance needed. The Top 10 is an awareness list of risk categories.
cards.explanation: Use the Top 10 to explain priorities and ASVS to define "done": pick a level, turn its requirements into acceptance criteria and test cases, and use it as the checklist for design and code reviews.

cards.prompt: What should a security-focused code review look for?
cards.answer: Follow untrusted data from every entry point to every sink (SQL, shell, HTML, file paths, deserialisation, redirects, outbound URLs); confirm an authorisation check on every object access; check secrets handling, cryptography use, error handling that fails closed, logging of sensitive data, and new dependencies.
cards.explanation: Automation (SAST, secret scanning, dependency review) handles the mechanical part; humans are better at authorisation logic and business-rule flaws, which tools barely see. Changes to authentication, authorisation, crypto or input parsing deserve a second security-minded reviewer.

resources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet — Secure Code Review

cards.prompt: What happens here when the permissions service is down?
cards.answer: The exception handler returns `True`, so an outage grants access to everyone — failing open. Security decisions must fail closed: deny on error, log it, and alert. OWASP 2025 lists mishandling of exceptional conditions as its own category for exactly this pattern.
cards.explanation: Failing open often comes from an understandable wish for availability. If the business decides some feature must degrade open, make that explicit, narrow and monitored — never an accident of a broad `except`.

resources.title: OWASP Top 10:2025 — A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions

cards.prompt: Where should application secrets live, and how should the application get them?
cards.answer: In a secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager), fetched at runtime by a workload identity — never in code, images or committed config. Prefer short-lived dynamic credentials (database users issued per deployment) that expire on their own, and design for rotation without redeploying.
cards.explanation: Environment variables are acceptable delivery but leak into crash dumps, child processes and debug pages. Scan repositories and CI logs for secrets, scope each secret to the one service that needs it, and log access to them.

cards.prompt: Which security properties should be covered by ordinary automated tests?
cards.answer: Authorisation: for each endpoint, tests proving another user's object returns 403/404 and an anonymous call returns 401. Also input-validation boundaries, security headers present, CSRF protection active, rate limits enforced, and dangerous features (debug endpoints) disabled in production builds.
cards.explanation: Access-control regressions are the most common serious bug class and the easiest to test for: a table of (role, endpoint, expected status) run in CI catches a forgotten decorator immediately. Add a regression test for every security bug fixed.

resources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet — Authorization Testing Automation
